summary: SNRI antidepressant for depression, generalized anxiety disorder, and pain conditions that overlap with mood, like fibromyalgia.
description: Duloxetine is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) used to treat depression, generalized anxiety disorder, and certain pain syndromes with strong mind–body overlap. It can lift mood, calm excessive worry, and reduce pain amplification, especially when tension, sleep disruption, and fatigue are part of the picture. Common side effects include nausea, dry mouth, sweating, sleep changes, and sexual dysfunction. More serious risks include liver injury, blood pressure changes, low sodium, and withdrawal symptoms if stopped too quickly. It should not be combined with MAOIs and must be used carefully with other serotonergic or blood-thinning medications.
patient_summary: Duloxetine (Cymbalta) is an antidepressant that helps with both emotional symptoms (like depression and generalized anxiety) and certain types of pain (like fibromyalgia or diabetic nerve pain) that often travel with mood problems. Most people take it once a day. It does not work instantly — benefits build over several weeks. Early on, nausea, dry mouth, sweating, or sleep changes are common. Some people notice sexual side effects. Rarely, it can affect the liver, blood pressure, or sodium levels in the blood. Never stop duloxetine suddenly; a slow, supervised taper is key to avoiding withdrawal symptoms such as dizziness and brain zaps.

primary.context: FDA-approved for adult unipolar depression. Often chosen when physical pain, fatigue, or poor response to an SSRI are part of the story.
FDA-approved for GAD in adults and children 7 years and older. Helpful when chronic worry shows up with muscle tension, restlessness, and poor sleep.
FDA-approved for fibromyalgia in adults and adolescents 13 years and older (specific formulations). Especially useful when widespread pain, non-restorative sleep, and low mood cluster together.
FDA-approved for chronic low back pain and osteoarthritis pain in adults. Often used when chronic pain, mood symptoms, and anxiety are tightly interwoven.
FDA-approved for neuropathic pain in adults; psychiatry may remain involved when nerve pain significantly worsens depression and anxiety.

off_label.context: Off-label in men and women when non-medication strategies are inadequate and mood or anxiety symptoms are also being treated.

therapeutic_response.display: Psychiatric benefit usually begins in 1–2 weeks, with fuller effect over 4–6 or more weeks.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Gastrointestinal upset (nausea, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhea)
common_adverse_effects.incidence: Nausea in roughly 18–25 percent of adults; other GI symptoms in about 5–15 percent
common_adverse_effects.notes: Nausea is one of the most common early issues. Taking duloxetine with food, starting at a lower dose such as 20–30 mg, and titrating slowly can help. Symptoms often improve after the first one to two weeks.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Insomnia or drowsiness in approximately 5–10 percent
common_adverse_effects.notes: Some people feel more activated and have trouble falling asleep; others feel more tired. Adjusting the time of day you take it, typically mornings, and working on sleep hygiene can help.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Reported in 3–10 percent in trials; real-world rates may be higher
common_adverse_effects.notes: Lower sex drive, difficulty getting or maintaining an erection, or delayed or absent orgasm are all possible. This is common and very discussable; dose changes, timing strategies, medication switches, or add-on treatments can help.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Sweating, hot flashes, and night sweats in at least 1–6 percent
common_adverse_effects.notes: Feeling overheated or sweaty is a common complaint, especially at higher doses. Hydration, layered clothing, and dose adjustments can help; if severe, another medication may be a better fit.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Blood pressure and heart rate effects
common_adverse_effects.incidence: Small increases observed in a minority of patients; hypertensive crisis is rare
common_adverse_effects.notes: Most people see little or no change, but if you already have high blood pressure or cardiovascular disease, regular monitoring is important, especially at doses above 60 mg per day.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Weight loss more common early on; modest weight gain later in some patients
common_adverse_effects.notes: Appetite may drop initially, leading to mild weight loss. Over time, as mood and appetite normalize, weight may return to baseline or increase slightly.

serious_risks.risk: Liver injury: New or worsening fatigue, dark urine, right upper abdominal pain, or yellowing of eyes or skin; this requires urgent evaluation and usually discontinuation of duloxetine.
Severe hyponatremia or SIADH: Confusion, severe headache, seizures, or increased falls; this is a medical emergency.
Serotonin syndrome: Agitation, confusion, sweating, fever, tremor, muscle rigidity, diarrhea, and rapid swings in blood pressure or heart rate; seek emergency care.
Severe skin reactions: Rash with blisters, peeling skin, or mucosal involvement (possible Stevens–Johnson syndrome); stop the medication and get urgent care.
Mania or hypomania: Markedly decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, grandiosity, or risky behavior, particularly in people with bipolar diathesis.

Severe withdrawal syndrome: After abrupt discontinuation, intense dizziness, brain zaps, nausea, irritability, and flu-like symptoms can occur; restarting and tapering slowly usually improves symptoms.
Increased suicidal thoughts or behaviors: Especially in children, adolescents, and young adults when starting or changing doses.

safety.black_box_warning: Monitor all antidepressant-treated patients, especially those 24 years and younger, for clinical worsening, suicidal thoughts, and unusual behavior changes during the first few months of treatment or after dose changes.

contraindications.contraindication: Current use of an MAOI intended to treat psychiatric disorders or use within the past 14 days
Starting an MAOI within at least 5 days of stopping duloxetine (many experts prefer 14 days)
Concurrent use of IV methylene blue intended for mood treatment
Known serious hypersensitivity to duloxetine or any capsule component
Chronic liver disease or cirrhosis (strongly discouraged due to higher hepatotoxicity risk)
Severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease (creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/minute) unless used at very low doses with expert oversight

precautions: Liver toxicity: Duloxetine has been linked to rare but serious liver injury, including hepatitis and liver failure. Risk is higher with chronic liver disease or heavy alcohol use.

Serotonin syndrome: Combining duloxetine with other serotonergic drugs (MAOIs, other antidepressants, certain migraine medications, tramadol, St. John’s wort, and others) can cause life-threatening serotonin syndrome.
Hyponatremia and SIADH: Duloxetine can cause low sodium levels, especially in older adults, people on diuretics, or those with a history of hyponatremia.
Blood pressure and heart rate: Small increases in blood pressure and pulse are possible; rare cases of hypertensive crisis have been reported.
Bleeding risk: SNRIs may increase bleeding, particularly when combined with NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants.
Activation of mania or hypomania: Can trigger mood elevation in people with bipolar disorder or bipolar spectrum risk, especially if used without a mood stabilizer.
Withdrawal symptoms: Abrupt discontinuation can cause dizziness, brain zaps, nausea, irritability, and flu-like symptoms; tapering is essential.

interactions.interactant: MAOIs such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, selegiline, and linezolid, as well as IV methylene blue
interactions.mechanism: Very high risk of life-threatening serotonin syndrome and blood pressure instability.
interactions.action: Contraindicated. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting duloxetine. Wait at least 5 days, and many experts prefer 14, after stopping duloxetine before starting an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Other serotonergic medications, including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, triptans, tramadol, many migraine and weight-loss medications, and St. John’s wort
interactions.mechanism: Additive serotonin effects with risk of serotonin syndrome.
interactions.action: Use combinations only when clearly indicated, at the lowest effective doses, with explicit education about serotonin syndrome symptoms and when to seek help.

interactions.interactant: Antiplatelets, anticoagulants, and NSAIDs such as aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants, ibuprofen, and naproxen
interactions.mechanism: Increased risk of gastrointestinal and other bleeding.
interactions.action: Monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, and gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms; consider gastroprotection or alternative agents when appropriate.

interactions.interactant: Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors such as fluvoxamine and drugs affecting CYP2D6 such as paroxetine, fluoxetine, some antipsychotics, and certain beta-blockers
interactions.mechanism: Altered duloxetine or co-medication levels, leading to increased side effects or loss of efficacy.
interactions.action: Use caution; consider lower starting doses, slower titration, and close monitoring for side effects or reduced effect of either medication.

interactions.interactant: Drugs that increase hyponatremia risk such as thiazide and loop diuretics, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and some antipsychotics
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of clinically significant low sodium and falls.
interactions.action: Check sodium at baseline and periodically, especially in older adults or those with prior hyponatremia or unexplained falls.

interactions.mechanism: Increased risk of liver injury when combined with duloxetine’s hepatic metabolism.
interactions.action: Avoid heavy alcohol and minimize other liver-toxic medications whenever possible; monitor liver function tests if combinations cannot be avoided.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidality and mood: Monitor for new or worsening suicidal thoughts, irritability, agitation, or mood swings, especially during the first 1–2 months and after dose changes.
Blood pressure and pulse: Check at baseline and periodically, particularly in patients with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or doses above 60 mg per day.
Liver function tests: Obtain at baseline and as clinically indicated, especially in those with liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or multiple hepatotoxic medications.
Serum sodium: Monitor in older adults, people on diuretics, those with prior hyponatremia, or those with unexplained confusion, falls, or seizures.
Renal function: Check at baseline and periodically if there is underlying kidney disease or use of other nephrotoxic drugs.
Blood glucose and HbA1c in diabetes: Monitor for small increases in glucose when duloxetine is used for diabetic neuropathy or in patients with diabetes and depression.
Signs of mania or hypomania: Screen for bipolar history before starting and monitor for decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, or risky behavior.
Bleeding risk: Assess for easy bruising, nosebleeds, or gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms, especially if combined with NSAIDs, aspirin, or anticoagulants.
Falls and gait: Monitor balance and falls, particularly in older adults or those with orthostatic symptoms or sedating co-medications.
Withdrawal symptoms: During dose reductions or missed doses, watch for dizziness, brain zaps, irritability, and flu-like symptoms; slow the taper if needed.

special_populations.pregnancy: Duloxetine crosses the placenta. Data so far do not show a dramatic birth defect signal, but there may be small increases in risks such as preeclampsia, spontaneous abortion, and postpartum hemorrhage. Third-trimester exposure may lead to neonatal adaptation syndrome, with jitteriness, feeding problems, and respiratory distress, and rarely persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. The bigger danger in many cases is untreated or undertreated depression and anxiety, which carries its own risk for preterm birth, low birth weight, and postpartum depression. For patients already stable and doing well on duloxetine before pregnancy, continuing the same medication is often safer than switching midstream. For treatment-naïve pregnant patients, SSRIs are usually first-line; duloxetine is more of a second-line option when pain and mood are both major concerns.
special_populations.lactation: Duloxetine appears in breast milk in very low concentrations, with relative infant doses typically under 1 percent of the maternal weight-adjusted dose. Infant serum levels are usually very low or undetectable in small reports. In practice, breastfeeding is generally compatible with duloxetine, especially if it was used successfully during pregnancy. Breastfed infants should be monitored for excessive sedation, poor feeding, or poor weight gain. For new starts in breastfeeding patients, other antidepressants may still be preferred, but duloxetine can be a reasonable choice when pain and mood are both targets.
special_populations.pediatric: Duloxetine is FDA-approved for generalized anxiety disorder in children and adolescents 7 years and older and for fibromyalgia in adolescents 13 years and older for specific formulations. Usual pediatric generalized anxiety disorder dosing starts at 30 mg once daily, increasing to 60 mg per day based on response and tolerability; doses up to 120 mg per day have been used under specialist supervision. For depression in youth, data are limited and duloxetine is not first-line; SSRIs such as fluoxetine and escitalopram have clearer evidence. As with all antidepressants in children and teens, close monitoring for suicidality, agitation, and behavioral activation is critical.
special_populations.geriatric: Older adults are more vulnerable to hyponatremia, falls, fractures, and blood pressure changes from SNRIs. Start low, typically 20–30 mg per day, titrate slowly, and aim for the lowest effective dose. Monitor sodium, blood pressure, gait, and cognition. Duloxetine appears in Beers and STOPP criteria as a medication to use cautiously in older adults with certain high-risk conditions such as recurrent falls, severe hypertension, or urinary issues.
special_populations.renal_impairment: In mild to moderate renal impairment with creatinine clearance at least 30 mL per minute, duloxetine can usually be used without formal dose adjustment, though lower starting doses are wise. In severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease, duloxetine and metabolites accumulate; most guidance recommends avoiding duloxetine or limiting to low doses with very close monitoring.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Duloxetine has a documented signal for drug-induced liver injury. It is generally avoided in moderate to severe hepatic impairment and in heavy alcohol use. If used despite mild liver disease due to lack of alternatives, lower maximum doses of 30 mg per day or less and frequent liver function testing are recommended. New or unexplained liver function test elevations, jaundice, or systemic symptoms should trigger discontinuation and evaluation.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed; food slightly delays peak levels and modestly lowers overall exposure but rarely matters clinically.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Moderate; duloxetine undergoes significant first-pass metabolism.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Approximately 5–6 hours after an oral dose.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Around 12 hours in adults, with a range of about 8–22 hours; somewhat longer in older women.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism via CYP1A2 and CYP2D6 to multiple inactive metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily in urine (around 70 percent, mostly as metabolites) and in feces (around 20 percent).
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Highly protein bound (greater than 90 percent) to albumin and alpha1-acid glycoprotein.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food delays time to peak by a few hours but has minimal impact on overall clinical effect.

dosing.titration: Duloxetine is usually taken once daily. For mood and anxiety, most people end up in the 30–60 mg per day range, with a maximum of 120 mg per day in carefully selected adults.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Duloxetine is a medication you taper, not one you simply stop. The goal is to lower the dose slowly enough that the brain has time to adjust.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Duloxetine is an SNRI that treats both emotional symptoms and certain pain conditions. It is most useful when depression, generalized anxiety, and physical pain are all tangled together.
items: Major Depressive Disorder (unipolar): Persistent low mood, loss of interest, negative thinking, fatigue, and hopelessness.
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD): Chronic, hard-to-control worry plus muscle tension, restlessness, and sleep disturbance.
Fibromyalgia with mood and sleep disturbance: Widespread pain, non-restorative sleep, brain fog, and often co-occurring depression or anxiety.
Chronic musculoskeletal pain with emotional distress: Chronic low back or neck pain and osteoarthritis pain in adults where pain is tightly linked to mood, anxiety, and sleep.
Neuropathic pain with psychological burden: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy in adults when nerve pain worsens sleep, mood, and functioning.
off_label: Stress urinary incontinence in men and women when non-medication approaches and pelvic floor work are not enough and depression is also present.
Adjunctive treatment in partial response depression or generalized anxiety disorder when pain, fatigue, and bodily tension remain prominent despite SSRIs or other antidepressants.
Perimenopausal mood and pain symptoms when SSRIs alone are inadequate and pain is a major driver of distress.

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: My baseline dread eased up — it was not gone, but it stopped running the show.
The anxiety did not disappear overnight, but the nonstop what if loop finally slowed down.
I noticed I could bounce back from stress instead of staying stuck there all day.
My muscles felt less clenched and the pain dialed down from unbearable to tolerable.
I still hurt, but I am not as emotionally crushed by the pain.
I could finally do small things again — walk the dog, unload the dishwasher — without crashing afterward.
items.note: Duloxetine rarely erases pain, but it can make pain less intense and less emotionally overwhelming.

quotes: The first week was rough — nausea, dry mouth, and feeling wired and tired at the same time.
I had a few days of headache and queasiness and then it started to level out.
Coffee plus duloxetine made me way more jittery early on; changing the timing helped.
items.note: Side effects tend to be loudest in the first one to two weeks. If they are severe or not improving, your prescriber needs to know.

quotes: I did not feel sedated, but the crushing fatigue from depression eased a bit.
Taking it in the morning helped with the slightly activated feeling.
My sleep was not magically fixed, but my mind was less busy at night.
My mood was better but my sex drive took a hit.
It was harder to reach orgasm even though my depression was lighter.
I felt more emotionally steady, but sometimes also a little blunted.
items.note: Sexual side effects are common with SNRIs and very worth talking about; we have options if this becomes a problem.

quotes: Missing a couple doses gave me dizziness and those weird electric brain zap sensations.
Stopping too fast felt like having the flu plus vertigo and mood swings.
When we slowed the taper, the withdrawal symptoms were way more manageable.
items.note: Duloxetine has a well-known withdrawal profile. Abrupt stops almost always backfire; a gradual taper is the safer path.

sections.intro: Experiences on duloxetine vary, but these are the patterns I hear most often in clinic:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Duloxetine is slow and steady, not immediate relief. It adjusts brain and body circuits gradually over weeks.
key_points: Depression: Early hints such as slightly better sleep, appetite, or energy may appear in 1–2 weeks; meaningful mood changes usually take 4–6 weeks.
Generalized anxiety disorder: Worry and physical tension often start to soften by 2–4 weeks, with full benefit sometimes taking 8–12 weeks.
Fibromyalgia and chronic pain: Improvements in pain, fatigue, and function usually emerge over several weeks and can continue to build for 2–3 months.
Daily rhythm: Once-daily dosing provides fairly stable 24-hour coverage; there is no fast hit or crash pattern.
Stopping: Levels fall gradually, but the nervous system can react quickly to drops, which is why slow, planned tapers are needed rather than sudden stops.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Duloxetine is a solid, middle-of-the-pack antidepressant in terms of raw mood and anxiety symptom reduction, but it becomes especially attractive when pain is part of the clinical picture. For many people, it does not just make them less sad; it helps them move, sleep, and function better in their bodies, which feeds back into mood and anxiety.
sections.metric: Response and remission in depression and generalized anxiety disorder
sections.comparison: Typically 10–20% higher response rates than placebo across depression and generalized anxiety disorder trials.
sections.clinical_details: Across randomized controlled trials in major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, duloxetine at 60–120 mg per day yields significantly higher response and remission rates compared with placebo. It also has evidence for fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain, and diabetic neuropathic pain, where it reduces pain severity and improves global functioning. Combining duloxetine with psychotherapy generally produces more robust and durable improvements than medication alone.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Antidepressants, including duloxetine, increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults.
sections.black_box: Monitor all antidepressant-treated patients, especially those 24 years and younger, for clinical worsening, suicidal thoughts, and unusual behavior changes during the first few months of treatment or after dose changes.
other: Liver toxicity: Duloxetine has been linked to rare but serious liver injury, including hepatitis and liver failure. Risk is higher with chronic liver disease or heavy alcohol use.

Serotonin syndrome: Combining duloxetine with other serotonergic drugs (MAOIs, other antidepressants, certain migraine medications, tramadol, St. John’s wort, and others) can cause life-threatening serotonin syndrome.
Hyponatremia and SIADH: Duloxetine can cause low sodium levels, especially in older adults, people on diuretics, or those with a history of hyponatremia.
Blood pressure and heart rate: Small increases in blood pressure and pulse are possible; rare cases of hypertensive crisis have been reported.
Bleeding risk: SNRIs may increase bleeding, particularly when combined with NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants.
Activation of mania or hypomania: Can trigger mood elevation in people with bipolar disorder or bipolar spectrum risk, especially if used without a mood stabilizer.
Withdrawal symptoms: Abrupt discontinuation can cause dizziness, brain zaps, nausea, irritability, and flu-like symptoms; tapering is essential.
patient_counseling: Tell your prescriber immediately if you notice new or worsening suicidal thoughts, agitation, or intense mood swings, especially in the first few months or after dose changes.
Avoid heavy alcohol use and be cautious if you have any history of liver disease; duloxetine and alcohol are a risky mix for the liver.
Never combine duloxetine with MAOIs and use great caution with other serotonin-boosting medications; this is how serotonin syndrome happens.
Report confusion, severe headache, balance problems, or seizures, as these can be signs of low sodium or other complications.
Let your doctor or dentist know you are on duloxetine before starting NSAIDs, blood thinners, or major procedures.
Do not stop duloxetine suddenly. Work with your prescriber on a gradual taper plan to minimize withdrawal symptoms.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most people notice some combination of nausea, dry mouth, sweating, sleep changes, or sexual side effects, especially in the first weeks. A smaller group develops clinically important changes in blood pressure, sodium, or liver function that need medical attention.
plain_language_list: Nausea, stomach upset, or decreased appetite, especially early on.
Sleep changes, including insomnia, vivid dreams, or sometimes feeling more sleepy.
Headache, dizziness, or feeling off or spacey.
Sexual side effects such as lower libido, delayed orgasm, or erectile difficulties.
Small weight changes, often mild weight loss at first and sometimes later weight gain.

sections.intro: Duloxetine interacts with medications that affect serotonin, bleeding risk, and liver metabolism. A full interaction check is mandatory before starting or changing doses.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Duloxetine is a medication you taper, not one you simply stop. The goal is to lower the dose slowly enough that the brain has time to adjust.
key_points: If you have been on duloxetine for at least 4 weeks, taper over at least 2–4 weeks; longer if you have been on it for months or years.
Higher-risk situations, such as long-term use, high doses, or prior withdrawal issues, may need very slow tapers over 2–3 or more months with dose reductions every 2–4 weeks.
Example taper from 60 mg per day: Step down to 40 mg daily for 1–2 weeks, then 30 mg for 1–2 weeks, then 20 mg for 1–2 weeks before stopping. Go slower if symptoms appear.
Common withdrawal symptoms include dizziness, brain zaps, nausea, irritability, anxiety, sweating, vivid dreams, and flu-like feelings.
If withdrawal gets intense, return to the last comfortable dose and taper more slowly rather than trying to push through.
Whenever possible, plan tapers for lower-stress times, not during major life events, finals, or big job changes.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Duloxetine is usually taken once daily. For mood and anxiety, most people end up in the 30–60 mg per day range, with a maximum of 120 mg per day in carefully selected adults.

adult.depression_initial: 40–60 mg per day, either as 20–30 mg twice daily or as a single 40–60 mg dose. For sensitive patients, start at 30 mg once daily for 1 week before increasing to 60 mg once daily.
adult.depression_titration: If partial response after at least 4 weeks at 60 mg per day, some experts increase by 30 mg increments, such as 90 mg then 120 mg, at intervals of 2–3 weeks as tolerated.
adult.depression_max: 120 mg per day; doses above 60 mg per day provide modest additional benefit and higher side-effect burden, and usually require specialist oversight.
adult.gad_initial: 60 mg once daily. For anxious or side-effect-sensitive patients, start at 30 mg once daily for 1–2 weeks, then increase to 60 mg once daily.
adult.gad_titration: If response is inadequate after 4–6 weeks at 60 mg per day, doses may be increased by 30 mg increments, for example to 90 mg then 120 mg per day, at intervals of at least 1 week in inpatient settings and more cautiously in outpatients.
adult.gad_max: 120 mg per day in adults, with close monitoring of blood pressure, sodium, and mood.
adult.fibromyalgia_initial: 30 mg once daily for 1 week, then increase to 60 mg once daily as tolerated; slower titration such as 20 mg to 40 mg to 60 mg can be used in very sensitive patients.
adult.fibromyalgia_max: 60 mg per day; higher doses up to 120 mg per day have been studied but often add side effects without clear added benefit.
adult.chronic_pain_initial: 30 mg once daily for 1–2 weeks for chronic low back pain or osteoarthritis, then increase to 60 mg once daily as tolerated.
adult.chronic_pain_max: 60 mg per day for most adults; some may trial up to 120 mg per day in specialist settings with careful monitoring.
adult.renal: Creatinine clearance at least 30 mL per minute: no formal adjustment, but consider lower starting doses such as 20–30 mg in frail patients. Creatinine clearance less than 30 mL per minute or end-stage renal disease: generally avoid; if absolutely necessary, use 30 mg once daily with very slow titration and do not exceed 60 mg per day.
adult.hepatic: Chronic liver disease or cirrhosis: generally avoid duloxetine. If there is no safer alternative and impairment is mild, some experts start at 30 mg once daily or less and avoid exceeding 30 mg per day, with frequent liver function monitoring.
adult.elderly: In adults 65 years and older, often start at 20–30 mg once daily and target 30–60 mg per day. Titrate slowly and keep at the lowest effective dose to reduce fall risk, hyponatremia, and blood pressure changes.

sections.simple_explanation: For most adults, duloxetine lives in the 30–60 mg per day zone. Some people go higher, up to 120 mg per day, if needed and well tolerated. Starting low and increasing slowly is the best way to control nausea, jitteriness, blood pressure changes, and withdrawal risk.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Duloxetine can be used safely in some special populations, but the threshold to start or continue it should be higher and monitoring tighter.
sections.pregnancy: Duloxetine crosses the placenta. Data so far do not show a dramatic birth defect signal, but there may be small increases in risks such as preeclampsia, spontaneous abortion, and postpartum hemorrhage. Third-trimester exposure may lead to neonatal adaptation syndrome, with jitteriness, feeding problems, and respiratory distress, and rarely persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. The bigger danger in many cases is untreated or undertreated depression and anxiety, which carries its own risk for preterm birth, low birth weight, and postpartum depression. For patients already stable and doing well on duloxetine before pregnancy, continuing the same medication is often safer than switching midstream. For treatment-naïve pregnant patients, SSRIs are usually first-line; duloxetine is more of a second-line option when pain and mood are both major concerns.
sections.lactation: Duloxetine appears in breast milk in very low concentrations, with relative infant doses typically under 1 percent of the maternal weight-adjusted dose. Infant serum levels are usually very low or undetectable in small reports. In practice, breastfeeding is generally compatible with duloxetine, especially if it was used successfully during pregnancy. Breastfed infants should be monitored for excessive sedation, poor feeding, or poor weight gain. For new starts in breastfeeding patients, other antidepressants may still be preferred, but duloxetine can be a reasonable choice when pain and mood are both targets.
sections.pediatrics: Duloxetine is FDA-approved for generalized anxiety disorder in children and adolescents 7 years and older and for fibromyalgia in adolescents 13 years and older for specific formulations. Usual pediatric generalized anxiety disorder dosing starts at 30 mg once daily, increasing to 60 mg per day based on response and tolerability; doses up to 120 mg per day have been used under specialist supervision. For depression in youth, data are limited and duloxetine is not first-line; SSRIs such as fluoxetine and escitalopram have clearer evidence. As with all antidepressants in children and teens, close monitoring for suicidality, agitation, and behavioral activation is critical.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are more vulnerable to hyponatremia, falls, fractures, and blood pressure changes from SNRIs. Start low, typically 20–30 mg per day, titrate slowly, and aim for the lowest effective dose. Monitor sodium, blood pressure, gait, and cognition. Duloxetine appears in Beers and STOPP criteria as a medication to use cautiously in older adults with certain high-risk conditions such as recurrent falls, severe hypertension, or urinary issues.
sections.hepatic: Duloxetine has a documented signal for drug-induced liver injury. It is generally avoided in moderate to severe hepatic impairment and in heavy alcohol use. If used despite mild liver disease due to lack of alternatives, lower maximum doses of 30 mg per day or less and frequent liver function testing are recommended. New or unexplained liver function test elevations, jaundice, or systemic symptoms should trigger discontinuation and evaluation.
sections.renal: In mild to moderate renal impairment with creatinine clearance at least 30 mL per minute, duloxetine can usually be used without formal dose adjustment, though lower starting doses are wise. In severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease, duloxetine and metabolites accumulate; most guidance recommends avoiding duloxetine or limiting to low doses with very close monitoring.
sections.other: Use extra caution in people with seizure disorders, uncontrolled hypertension, significant fall risk, or narrow-angle glaucoma. After bariatric surgery, absorption of delayed-release capsules can be unpredictable; other antidepressants may be safer and more reliable.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and mood: Monitor for new or worsening suicidal thoughts, irritability, agitation, or mood swings, especially during the first 1–2 months and after dose changes.
Blood pressure and pulse: Check at baseline and periodically, particularly in patients with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or doses above 60 mg per day.
Liver function tests: Obtain at baseline and as clinically indicated, especially in those with liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or multiple hepatotoxic medications.
Serum sodium: Monitor in older adults, people on diuretics, those with prior hyponatremia, or those with unexplained confusion, falls, or seizures.
Renal function: Check at baseline and periodically if there is underlying kidney disease or use of other nephrotoxic drugs.
Blood glucose and HbA1c in diabetes: Monitor for small increases in glucose when duloxetine is used for diabetic neuropathy or in patients with diabetes and depression.
Signs of mania or hypomania: Screen for bipolar history before starting and monitor for decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, or risky behavior.
Bleeding risk: Assess for easy bruising, nosebleeds, or gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms, especially if combined with NSAIDs, aspirin, or anticoagulants.
Falls and gait: Monitor balance and falls, particularly in older adults or those with orthostatic symptoms or sedating co-medications.
Withdrawal symptoms: During dose reductions or missed doses, watch for dizziness, brain zaps, irritability, and flu-like symptoms; slow the taper if needed.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: All current duloxetine products are delayed-release capsules designed to protect the drug from stomach acid and release it further down the gastrointestinal tract.
items: Delayed-release capsules (Cymbalta and generics): 20 mg, 30 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg.
Delayed-release sprinkle capsules (Drizalma Sprinkle and generics): 20 mg, 30 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg, which can be opened and sprinkled on applesauce when swallowing capsules is difficult.
Important: Capsules should not be crushed or chewed. Sprinkle formulations can be opened, but the individual pellets must not be crushed or chewed or the enteric coating will be damaged.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Duloxetine blocks the reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine, two key neurotransmitters involved in mood, anxiety, and pain pathways. By increasing their availability in the synapse, duloxetine strengthens descending inhibitory signals that dampen pain and stabilizes circuits that regulate mood, worry, and arousal. It has minimal direct activity at histamine, cholinergic, or adrenergic receptors, and it does not act as a monoamine oxidase inhibitor.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In modern guidelines, duloxetine is considered a first- or second-line antidepressant option for adults, especially when pain is part of the clinical picture. For straightforward depression or anxiety without major pain, SSRIs are often tried first due to long-term safety data and simplicity. Duloxetine becomes particularly appealing when there is clear comorbid fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, or chronic back or neck pain; when a prior SSRI trial produced only partial improvement; or when fatigue, physical tension, and pain are major drivers of distress. It also serves as a reasonable maintenance agent once a good response is achieved, often continued for at least 6–12 months after remission, and longer in recurrent or severe illness. As with all antidepressants, combining duloxetine with psychotherapy typically produces better and more durable outcomes than medication alone.

faqs.q: What is duloxetine (Cymbalta) used for in mental health?
faqs.a: Duloxetine is an SNRI antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and certain pain conditions such as fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain, and diabetic nerve pain that often travel with mood and anxiety issues. It is a particularly good option when emotional and physical symptoms are feeding into each other.

faqs.q: How long does it take for duloxetine to start working?
faqs.a: You may notice small shifts such as slightly better sleep, a bit more energy, or less mental noise within 1–2 weeks. Clearer changes in mood and anxiety usually show up after 4–6 weeks. Pain-related benefits may take 6–12 weeks to fully show. If nothing at all has changed by around week 4, it is worth checking in with your prescriber about dose and strategy.

It can do either, depending on your biology and dose. Some people feel more awake and focused, which can be helpful for depression and fatigue. Others feel more tired or foggy. If duloxetine is activating, taking it in the morning usually helps. If it is sedating, your prescriber can adjust the dose or consider alternative options.

faqs.q: Can duloxetine help with both pain and mood?
faqs.a: Yes. Duloxetine is one of the few antidepressants with strong evidence for both emotional symptoms and certain pain syndromes. By boosting serotonin and norepinephrine, it helps strengthen the brain’s natural pain-dampening pathways and stabilizes mood and anxiety circuits. It rarely wipes out pain altogether, but it can lower the intensity and make pain less emotionally overwhelming.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of duloxetine?
faqs.a: Common side effects include nausea, stomach upset, dry mouth, sweating, sleep changes, headache, and sexual side effects such as lower libido or delayed orgasm. Many early side effects improve after 1–2 weeks. If they are intense, persistent, or interfere with daily life, talk with your prescriber about dose changes or alternatives.

faqs.q: Does duloxetine cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: It can. Duloxetine may lower sex drive, make it harder to get or maintain an erection, or delay or prevent orgasm. This is very common with serotonin-based antidepressants and absolutely something to bring up. There are strategies to help, including dose timing, dose adjustments, adding a counteracting medication, or switching to a different antidepressant.

Duloxetine is not a controlled substance and does not cause addiction in the way benzodiazepines or opioids do. However, your brain does adapt to it, which means stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms like dizziness, brain zaps, irritability, and flu-like feelings. That is why a slow, supervised taper is crucial when you and your prescriber decide it is time to stop.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop duloxetine too fast?
faqs.a: Stopping abruptly or tapering too quickly can cause a withdrawal syndrome: dizziness, electric shock sensations in the head often called brain zaps, nausea, irritability, anxiety, and sleep problems. These symptoms can be very uncomfortable but are usually reversible. The typical fix is to go back to the last dose you tolerated well and then taper more slowly with your prescriber’s guidance.

faqs.q: Is duloxetine safe if I have liver or kidney problems?
faqs.a: Duloxetine is heavily processed by the liver, and serious liver injury, though rare, has been reported. It is usually avoided in people with significant chronic liver disease or heavy alcohol use. In severe kidney disease or dialysis, drug levels increase, so most experts avoid duloxetine or use only low doses with close monitoring. If you have liver or kidney issues, your prescriber may favor other antidepressants with safer metabolic profiles unless the potential benefit of duloxetine clearly outweighs the risk.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking duloxetine?
faqs.a: Light, occasional alcohol is not absolutely forbidden for everyone, but alcohol plus duloxetine increases liver strain and can worsen sedation, balance, and mood. Heavy alcohol use is a clear red flag and significantly increases liver risk. If you drink, keep it minimal, avoid binge drinking, and be upfront with your prescriber about your alcohol use so they can help you weigh risks and benefits.

Early in treatment, duloxetine is more likely to cause mild weight loss because of nausea and reduced appetite. Over time, as mood and appetite normalize, some people regain that weight or gain a small amount above baseline. Large weight changes are less common than with some other psychiatric medications but can happen. Tracking weight, appetite, and activity can help you and your prescriber respond early if weight becomes an issue.

faqs.q: How is duloxetine different from an SSRI like sertraline or fluoxetine?
faqs.a: SSRIs mainly affect serotonin, while duloxetine affects both serotonin and norepinephrine. In everyday practice, this means duloxetine may be particularly helpful for patients whose depression or anxiety is tightly linked to physical pain, fatigue, and body tension. SSRIs are usually first-line for straightforward depression and anxiety; duloxetine is often chosen when there is a prominent pain component or when an SSRI alone has not been enough.

faqs.q: Can duloxetine trigger mania or hypomania?
faqs.a: Yes. Like other antidepressants, duloxetine can flip mood into hypomania or mania in people with bipolar disorder or bipolar risk. That is why it is critical to screen for personal or family history of bipolar disorder, and to watch for signs like decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, unusual energy, or risky behavior. If these occur, contact your clinician quickly; treatment usually involves stopping or adjusting the antidepressant and starting or optimizing a mood stabilizer.
